lesson_title: Pass the Proton: Acids, Bases and the Colours That Betray Them
hook_text: Ammonia is a base with zero hydroxide in its formula. Chemistry's best trick question, solved in one pass.
clip_script: Here's chemistry's favourite trick question: ammonia, NH3, is definitely a base — it turns litmus blue, it neutralises acids. But look at its formula. No hydroxide. No oxygen. No metal. The old textbook definition says bases carry hydroxide... so how is this a base at all? Answer: stop reading formulas and watch the game. Acid-base chemistry is pass-the-ball, and the ball is a single proton. The thrower is the acid. The catcher is the base. Drop ammonia into water and watch: WATER throws its proton, ammonia catches it and becomes NH4 plus — and the robbed water molecule? It's left as OH minus. Hydroxide. Ammonia didn't bring hydroxide to the party; it made hydroxide out of the water it mugged. That's the whole modern definition: donors and catchers. And water is the double agent — it catches from strong throwers like HCl, and throws to keen catchers like ammonia. Same molecule, both roles. Once you watch the ball instead of the jerseys, every equation in this topic reads itself.
visual_style: Molecules as jersey-wearing players passing a glowing proton; ammonia intercepting a pass from a water molecule that flashes into OH minus; water shown split-screen playing for both teams.
mood: Mischievous and clarifying — a trick question dismantled in real time.
pacing: Trick question up front, a pause on the impossible formula, fast pass-the-ball reveal, cool double-agent close.
